| DEF237 | 2026-08-08 | room | **The geometry annotation has no plausibility backstop, so a mis-parsed price level renders a fabricated downside under "These are the figures of record".** Found by the **independent auditor in DEF235 round 1** (`orchestration/audit/cr/DEF235.auditor.md`), attacking a claim that defect's submission made and could not support; confirmed live and then widened against the real corpus. DEF235 removed the `size` prose-parse because it read an entry price as a position size. Its submission argued the surviving `entry`/`stop`/`target` patterns were **not the same risk class**, because *"a mis-parse cannot silently rescale a figure — the triple must form a valid long setup before anything renders."* **That reasoning is false and is withdrawn.** The auditor's counter-example, reproduced exactly: `"Entry $180.00, stop cut to near 3% under, target $220.00"` → `_match_level` returns entry 180.0, **stop 3.0** (the pattern scans forward through *", stop cut to near "* — 13 digit-free chars, inside the 15-char window — and captures the `3` of `3%`), target 220.0. `risk_reward` is the ONLY gate, and it checks **ordering, not plausibility**: `3.00 < 180.00 < 220.00` passes, so AMI renders *"R:R 0.2:1; 22.2% upside vs **98.3% downside**; drawdown contribution ≈ 2.95 pt … These are the figures of record."* A debator narrating a stop being tightened is completely ordinary Room prose. **Not hypothetical — two live instances already sit in the committed epoch corpus** (`CR143_agent_prompt_audit/corpus/room_runs_2026-08-07-epoch.json`, 216 turns; of the **19** turns where `stop` matched at all, **2 (10.5%) captured a number implausible against the entry**): the AMD Conservative Debator yields `entry=4.0, stop=464.65` — `entry` fires on *"Cap the initial **entry** at **4.0%**"*, a size percentage, while `stop` correctly captures the real *"hard stop at $464.65"* — and the GRAB Neutral Debator yields a **full triple** `entry=2.0, stop=3.45, target=44.0`. Neither rendered, and **neither was stopped by a guard**: AMD had no target, and GRAB's `3.45 > 2.0` inverted the ordering. Both were luck. **Correction, DEF235 round-2 audit MINOR 2 — read this before fixing:** an earlier version of this row claimed the GRAB triple was *"parsed out of a leaked `[STANCE: … HEADLINE: 2.0% size, $3.50 stop]` envelope — the CR155 stance-leak feeding this parser its levels."* **That is false.** The auditor located the match spans instead of trusting the attribution, and re-verified here: the envelope occupies chars 60–128, while the three matches land at 390 (`**Size & Entry:** Scale to **2.0%**`), 577 (`**Stop-Loss:** Set stop at **$3.45**` — the debator's real stop) and 807 (`**$5.89** target upside (**44%**)`). The envelope's own `$3.50 stop` is never even reached: `\bstop(?:[\s-]*loss)?\b` matches `Stop-Loss` first, but the 18 non-digit chars to `$3.45` exceed the 15-char cap, so that attempt fails and `.search()` moves on. **Fixing the CR155 leak would close neither instance.** The real causes are broader and independent of it: a combined bullet header (`Size & Entry:`) puts a level label next to a size percentage, and — the sharper one — `target` captured `44` from *"**$5.89** target upside (**44%**)"* where the actual $5.89 target sits immediately **before** the label and the pattern only ever reads forward. A backward-looking `$`-anchor is worth considering alongside the plausibility gate. **The fix is not a tighter regex** — that is the DEF234 treadmill, and DEF231-233 spent six rounds proving it on a simpler pattern. It is the backstop `_annotate_rr_against_levels` never got: compare each extracted level against the run's structured `profile["last_close"]` and **refuse to annotate at all** when any of them is implausibly far from it, exactly as `_direction_contradictions` already does with `_DIRECTION_MAX_PLAUSIBLE_GAP_PCT = 400.0`, whose own comment names itself *"the backstop for the NEXT parse defect in the same class"*. **Two design decisions that make this a defect of its own rather than a one-line reuse, and why it was NOT folded into DEF235 round 2:** (1) that constant's gap formula `100*(close-level)/level` is **asymmetric** — a level 13.8× the close (GRAB's `target=44.0` against a $3.18 stock) evaluates to −92.8% and passes a 400% threshold, so a symmetric ratio is needed and the threshold must be re-derived for it; (2) with only **5 full triples in 216 turns** the corpus cannot validate a threshold, and a number chosen against the examples that motivated it is precisely `failure_patterns` **P16**. Refusing to annotate is the designed failure mode (a miss costs nothing; a confident fabricated 98.3% downside costs the surface its credibility) — the same trade DEF234 already made. Scope: `_verify_and_annotate_geometry` gains the close, `_annotate_rr_against_levels` gains the guard, threshold derived from data and stated as measured. Related: DEF235 (the `size` half, fixed); DEF236 (the format-vs-parser conflict that keeps levels in running prose — this defect is the backstop, DEF236 is the cause); CR155 (the stance leak that supplies one of the two live instances). **FIXED 2026-08-11 (AT:R68), Batch 2 of the CR143 remediation programme, shipped beside DEF242 because that widening is what makes this backstop load-bearing.** **The threshold is DERIVED, not chosen, and not fitted to the corpus.** The sibling DEF231 check already carried one — `abs(gap_pct) > 400` where `gap_pct = 100 × (close − level) / level` — and the algebra shows it only ever guarded ONE direction: that resolves to `close > 5 × level` and to nothing else, because the other branch needs `close/level < −3`, which no pair of positive prices reaches. So a level far BELOW the close (DEF234's comma bug, $1,073.46 → 1.0) tripped it at 107900%, while a level 13.8× the close evaluated to −92.8% and sailed through. `_MAX_PLAUSIBLE_LEVEL_RATIO = 5.0` is 400% restated symmetrically via `max(level/close, close/level)`, so the already-guarded side keeps exactly its behaviour and only the uncaught side gains it; the old constant is kept solely as the derivation and nothing reads it. It is deliberately NOT tuned — 216 turns hold 5 full triples, which cannot validate a threshold (P16), and a number fitted to five examples would read as evidence-backed while being nothing of the sort. **Scope as the row specified:** `_verify_and_annotate_geometry` gains `reference_close`, supplied at the call site from the existing `_reference_close(ctx.profile)` — itself gated on `field_state["technicals"] == LIVE`, so a run without recorded provenance passes None and the check degrades to its pre-fix behaviour rather than comparing against a number of unknown origin (CR104). | DEF239 | 2026-08-08 | room | **A PM verdict that stated its reasoning under the wrong JSON key ships to the user carrying AMI's "it wrote no rationale" disclosure — a false statement about AMI's own work, in AMI's own voice.** Found by the CR143 prompt audit (CR156). `_parse_pm_verdict` reads `narration`; the base prompt's own profile block teaches a `Reasoning:` label, and the model reaches for neighbouring keys. The PM wrote three sentences of reasoning; AMI told the user it wrote none, and the record now says so forever. **1 of 18 in the epoch (5.6%).** The disclosure itself is correct behaviour for a genuinely unexplained decision (that is DEF232's work) — the defect is that a key-name miss is indistinguishable from silence. **Fix direction:** accept the reasoning from any of the small set of keys the model actually reaches for (`rationale`/`reasoning`/`reason`), or stop teaching a second label in the profile block, or both; and make the no-rationale disclosure fire only when the reply carries **no** prose under any key. Do NOT widen it into a general free-text scrape — `_PM_NO_RATIONALE` exists because an unexplained decision must stay visible, and a fix that recovers prose from anywhere would hide the case it was written for. Verify against the 811-row `pm_verdict_corpus.txt` before shipping (P16), and re-derive the 5.6% after: the epoch's first-pass parse rate is otherwise **18/18**, so this is currently the only PM-parse defect on the current prompt. | DEF240 | 2026-08-08 | room | **When a mandate permits full concentration, the Room advocates it without ever saying what it means — AMI should state the number out loud.** **Saiful's ruling, 2026-08-08**, asked as a product question out of the CR143 prompt audit after the same issue surfaced independently in three per-agent reviews (CR149, CR153, CR154): *"Keep it, but make AMI say the number out loud."* **Nothing here is broken vs. the mandate.** `day_trader_preset.py` really does set `single_name_cap_pct: 100.0`; `_risk_tier_size_ceiling` → `resolved_single_name_cap_pct` is the same resolver `enforce_safety_floor` clamps to, so shown == enforced, and the auditor confirmed the preset is real and reachable rather than a hypothetical. **Measured: 7 of 18 epoch convenes ran under a 100.0% single-name cap** (re-derived from the 216 stored `system_prompt` rows at 12 turns per convene — 84 turns at 100.0%, 120 at 3.0%, 12 at 10.0%; an earlier count of 6 was low by one and is corrected). Under those mandates the agents behave correctly and the result reads alarming: the Bull Researcher proposed **50% of portfolio in one name**, and on SNOA the Aggressive Debator advocated *"100% of portfolio"* into a book already **95.8% GME with $422.50 cash**. **The defect is disclosure, not enforcement.** A simulator whose whole purpose is teaching lets a user watch a 12-analyst team argue for a 50% single-name position while every rendered figure stays neutral about what that concentration is. The remedy is CR040's own question inverted — *if this ships constantly and quietly, what does the user end up believing?* — so: whenever a mandate permits more than 25% in one name, AMI states the concentration in plain terms on the PM verdict and in the geometry annotation, alongside the drawdown contribution DEF235 already renders (*"at the mandate's 100.0% single-name cap"*). **Explicitly NOT in scope: capping the preset, or capping the rendered number.** Both were considered and rejected — overriding a mandate the user chose is a different product decision, and a ceiling on a *reported* figure is exactly how DEF235 shipped a wrong one. Loud and correct beats quiet and comfortable. **Do not implement this as a prompt instruction** (CLAUDE.md: prompt instructions are not controls, ~30% compliance); it is a rendered string on a deterministic branch. Acceptance: a convene under a 100% cap shows the concentration statement, a convene under 3.0% does not, the threshold is asserted at both sides, and the per-agent baselines from CR143 are re-measured post-promotion. **FIXED 2026-08-08.** `_concentration_note(size_pct, cap_pct)` renders one factual sentence above `_LOUD_CONCENTRATION_PCT = 25.0` — *"(Concentration: this is 50.0% of the portfolio in one name. Your mandate's single-name cap is 100.0%, so the safety floor permits it.)"* — appended to the PM's `verdict.reason` (the string CR106 renders as the decision's justification) and, as a second clause, to the geometry annotation the user watches stream. **It states the ENFORCED size, not the requested one:** the append sits after the risk-tier clamp, so a PM asking 90% under a 40% cap is disclosed at 40% — stating the request would describe a position the user never gets, which is DEF235's failure in a new place. **25% is a disclosure threshold, not a risk limit** — four equal names is the point past which one company's outcome, rather than a portfolio's, is what the book tracks — and it gates a sentence, never a decision (DEF059: the floor stays the sole vetoer; `test_def240_never_changes_the_verdict` pins the trade still APPROVEs). **Factual, never advisory — and the round-1 audit MAJOR was exactly here.** The clause first shipped as *"…so the safety floor permits it"* and the auditor, asked to read for tone rather than scan for banned words, found it crosses: "permits" is an **authorization verb**, carrying the same connotation as *"the law permits it"* — not merely *this breaks no rule* but *this is sanctioned*. A user who has just watched twelve analysts argue for half their portfolio in one name, then reads that the floor permits it, is handed a recommendation-shaped inference for free. The sibling disclosures are the standard it failed against: *"(sized down to 40.0% — mandate risk-tier ceiling.)"* states **what happened**; "permits" states an evaluative **outcome**. Both true; only one is a disclosure. Now: *"Your mandate's single-name cap is 100.0%; this position does not exceed it."* — the user still learns why it was not blocked, without being told it is therefore a good idea. **The word-list test could never have caught this** and says so in its own docstring: "permits" was not advice-shaped in isolation, only as the sentence's conclusion. The list now also bars *permits/permitted/allows/allowed/approved/sanctioned/cleared/acceptable/is fine/is safe*, but it is a regression floor, not the check — the check is a human reading the sentence, which is what the audit was for. A missing cap degrades to the share alone rather than swallowing the disclosure. **Mutation proof, 10 of 10 killed** — never appended; moved above the clamp so it reports the request; threshold at 100 (fires on nothing) and at 0 (fires on everything, i.e. boilerplate); boundary flipped to inclusive; a missing cap swallowing the note; the sentence turned advisory; the geometry clause deleted; **the round-1 authorization wording restored** (the MAJOR, exactly); and the cap clause dropped entirely, which would leave the user unable to tell why the trade was not blocked. **Two survived the first pass and are worth recording:** the geometry-annotation clause had NO test at all (MUT-8 passed with all ten other tests green — the ruling names two surfaces and I had covered one), and my first MUT-2 was inert, adding an unused variable rather than changing behaviour, so it proved nothing until rewritten to actually move the append above the clamp. Related: CR149/CR153/CR154 (the three independent sightings), DEF235 (the annotation this rides on), CR129/DEF187 (which removed the 50% absolute fallback from the floor). **ACCEPTANCE DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED — the branch is unreachable in production for a legitimate reason, and that is the finding.** Attempted 2026-08-11 with a mandate carrying an explicit `single_name_cap_pct: 100.0`, which puts the 25% threshold well in reach, against a real portfolio holding 30.1% MSFT. So the disclosure fires only when the PM approves more than a quarter of the portfolio in one name, and the model does not do that **even when the mandate explicitly permits 100%** — the debators argued toward the cap and the PM moderated the Trader's 8.0% down to 5.0%. The unit tests cover the branch; a live exercise would need a verdict I cannot obtain without fabricating one, and fabricating the input to an acceptance test is the opposite of paying it. Recorded as unexercised-in-production rather than passed, and worth knowing on its own: the loud-concentration guard is protecting against a size this model essentially never proposes. | fixed | — | AT:R66 |

(a) is smaller, removes a whole class of unverifiable claims, and costs the Bull a conclusion CR149 measured as reaching **32 of 811 real PM verdict reasons**; (b) preserves it and needs a mechanism that does not exist yet. | DEF245 | 2026-08-09 | room | **A worked example in the Bear's prompt carried a literal `-25%`, and it became the most common downside figure AMI has ever told a user.** Found by CR150 during the CR143 prompt audit. `content/agents/bear_researcher.md` modelled the quantify-downside instruction as *"if X happens, we're looking at **-25%**, and X is more likely than consensus thinks because…"* — a hard number three lines above a grounding directive forbidding exactly that. **Measured against `backend/tests/unit/fixtures/pm_verdict_corpus.txt`**, the frozen P16 fixture holding every real Alpha `room_runs.verdict->>'reason'` carrying a `$` figure (811 deduplicated rows): **22 verdicts (2.7%) contain `-25%`, 12 of them attributing it to the Bear** — *"the Bear's -25% downside to $53"*, *"the bear case for a -25% drawdown to $11.00"* — and `-25%` is the **single most frequent downside magnitude in the entire population** (18 occurrences in downside context against 7 for the next value). Verdict `reason` is what CR106 renders as the decision's justification and what `build_journal_entry_for_run` writes to the permanent Decision Journal, so the placeholder reached the record with an attribution to an agent that never derived it. **The generalisation, from CR149, is what makes this fixable rather than whack-a-mole:** *an example only leaks into the slot its instruction cannot otherwise fill.* The Bull's `32.4% gross margins` example appears **0 times** in 216 epoch turns and 0 times in the 811 verdicts — because that slot has data behind it. Mandate values (cap/ceiling/max/limit) are excluded: those are configuration, not a modelled outcome. **Mutation proof, 6 of 6 killed** across DEF244+DEF245, including restoring the literal and growing one on a different agent. **Acceptance owes a post-promotion re-measure:** `-25%` occurrences in new verdicts should fall to ~0, and the distribution of downside magnitudes should widen rather than concentrate — if it merely concentrates on a *different* number, the instruction is still doing the model's work for it and the remedy was wrong. Related: CR150 (found it), CR149 (the generalisation that predicts which examples leak), DEF244 (shipped together), CR038 (prompt instructions are not controls — this is why the example, not the prohibition, was the lever). **RESIDUAL I INTRODUCED, found and fixed by track R68 (`19cb0e3c`, CR145 Tier A) — recorded because this row otherwise implies the replacement was sound.** Removing the literal was right; what I put in its place was not. `fundamentals_analyst.md` went from *"strong margins → 32.4% gross margins, up 180bps YoY"* to *"gross margins at the level the fact sheet states, and the direction it is moving"* — and the fact sheet renders neither. `fundamentals.py` computes `profitMargins`, which is **net**, labelled as such since DEF053's own fix, and it carries **no margin trend at all**. | DEF247 | 2026-08-09 | room | **One conversational line ahead of the stance envelope makes the Room print its own machine channel to the user — and lose the stance chip.** Found by the **post-promotion re-measure of DEF241/DEF243** (batch `cr143-postpromo-smoke-20260809`, 3 tickers × 12 agents = 36 `llm_audit` rows, user `f73bb9d1`, all on the new prompt epoch — every agent stamped a distinct `prompt_version`, CR158 working). **3 of 9 debator turns rendered the raw `[STANCE: for \| CONVICTION: high \| HEADLINE: 0.30pt drawdown cost for elite growth]` line verbatim in the middle of the prose**, and all three parsed to `stance=None`, dropping into the comb's §3.4 "did not state a view" gutter while the machine channel they failed to yield sat visible two lines above it. Verified by running the shipped `parse_stance_envelope` over the stored `response_text` — not inferred from a pattern. **This is not a DEF243 regression, but my first account of why was wrong and is corrected here.** I wrote — in this row, in the audit submission, and to Saiful — that *"DEF243 removed the `Open with:` instruction; `grep -i \"open with\"` over the three debator prompts returns nothing"*, and concluded the opener was model drift against an unambiguous instruction, tagging the emission side **model-ceiling**. **That grep was wrong and so was the conclusion.** DEF243 (`719d2e48`) **reworded** the line, it did not remove it: `conservative_debator.md:23` reads *"Open your PROSE with: \"I'd argue for [smaller / shorter / hedged / wait]\" — the stance line comes first, on its own line above it (see the format block)"*, and the aggressive and neutral prompts carry the same shape. The literal string `open with` never appears because the word `PROSE` sits inside it. **So the model is not drifting — it is obeying, and mis-ordering two instructions it was given.** The correct class is **P4, contradictory instruction sets across prompt layers**: the base prompt says open with this sentence, `_STANCE_FORMAT` says the envelope is the VERY FIRST line, and DEF243's remedy was a parenthetical disambiguation — which is exactly the "another emphatic sentence buys ~30%" move CR038 says does not work. Measured after that disambiguation: it did not work. The emission side is therefore **prompt-fixable**, not model-ceiling; it belongs to DEF251, and the DEF244 precedent (cut the demand, name its owner) is the likely remedy. **The leak, however, is ours.** `parse_stance_envelope` ([room_runner.py:1949-1979](backend/app/services/room_runner.py#L1949-L1979)) considers exactly two candidate positions — `filled[0]` and `filled[-1]` — and its only fallback, `_STANCE_TAIL_RE`, is `\Z`-anchored by design. Related: DEF147 (put the envelope at the front and decoupled strip from parse), DEF243 (removed the competing `Open with:` line — shipped, confirmed present in the deployed bytes), DEF241 (same batch; **paid** — Aggressive quoted its own `0.30 pt`, Conservative its own `0.09 pt` and argued against *"the full 0.18 pt implied by the trader's 3.0%"*), CR143 Phase 4b (the model arm this is evidence for), CR106 §2.2 (why a stance is never inferred from prose). **FIXED 2026-08-10, and the rate is now measured rather than asserted.** The strip stops being positional (`found = [i for i in filled if _STANCE_LINE_RE.match(lines[i])]`); front still wins, `_STANCE_TAIL_RE` untouched, plus a `\n{3,}` collapse so the removed line does not leave a hole and a `room_stance_envelope_displaced` log key so the emission rate stays countable after the leak is closed. **Baseline batch `cr143-def247-baseline-20260810`, 31 of 32 tickers completed (WU failed, re-runnable), 420 `llm_audit` rows, 105 debator turns, measured by reimplementing the SHIPPED parser explicitly** (the first pass reported 0% because it ran the local working tree, which already carried the fix — corrected before publication): **35 of 105 turns (33.3%) leak the machine channel into user-visible prose, 56 (53.3%) yield no stance at all, only 49 (46.7%) are correct.** The fix converts every one of the 35, taking parsed-stance yield to **80.0%**. **Mutation proof 7 of 7 killed**; | DEF248 | 2026-08-10 | prompt | process | **A `<test-cmd>` that changes directory defeats `mutation_guard.sh`'s revert, and `set -e` kills the check written to catch exactly that — P9 inside the script built to prevent P9.** Surfaced while proving CR162's new semantics-identifier guard was real: `scripts/mutation_guard.sh mobile/lib/widgets/hex/hex_bottom_nav.dart "<perl mutation>" "cd mobile && flutter test test/qa/semantics_ids_test.dart"`. The mutation applied, the tests went red (the guard works), and then the revert printed `error: pathspec 'mobile/lib/widgets/hex/hex_bottom_nav.dart' did not match any file(s) known to git` — **leaving the mutation applied in the working tree with nothing saying so**. Root cause: `eval "$TEST_CMD"` ran in the script's *own* shell rather than a subshell, so `cd mobile` moved the script's cwd and the repo-relative `git checkout -- "$TARGET"` no longer resolved. The second-order failure is the serious one — the script runs under `set -euo pipefail`, so the failing checkout **exited the script immediately**, making `if ! git diff --quiet -- "$TARGET"; then fail "revert INCOMPLETE …"` unreachable dead code in the single situation it was written for. The script's stated promise — *"prove the revert was total by reading the tree, not by trusting the command"* — did not hold. **The failure mode is quiet**: the operator sees `── test exit code under mutation: 1` (reads as "caught"), then a git error that looks like tidy-up noise; a run that went straight on to `flutter test` would have reported a red suite against a silently mutated tree, or the mutation would have been swept into the next commit — and on this shared checkout, attributed to whichever lane committed next. Mirror-image of the incidents `mutation_guard.sh`'s own header documents: DEF127/DEF130 were *"the revert deleted something it shouldn't have"*, this is *"the revert never happened"*. **Fixed** in `scripts/mutation_guard.sh`: (1) `REPO_ROOT` resolved once and every git call pinned to it via a `git()` wrapper, so cwd cannot affect whether a revert lands; (2) `TARGET` absolutised before any git call so the cwd-relative `-e` test and the repo-root-pinned git calls can never disagree about which file is meant (verified `ls-files --error-unmatch` still correctly rejects an untracked absolute path, so DEF127's tracked-file precondition is intact); (3) `$MUTATE` and `$TEST_CMD` both wrapped in subshells so a `cd` in either cannot move the script; (4) the checkout's exit status captured rather than fatal, so `set -e` can no longer skip the tree comparison — which is now authoritative and, on failure, names the still-applied mutation and prints the restore command. **Verified by re-running the exact command that lost the mutation**: `✅ mutation caught (exit 1), tree restored`, script exit 0, `git diff --quiet` clean; plus a subdirectory invocation with a subdir-relative path, and confirmation that the `-x`/`--exitfirst` (DEF136) and untracked-target (DEF127) preconditions still fire. Related: CR110 (built the script), DEF127, DEF130, DEF136, `failure_patterns.md` P9, CR162 (the work that surfaced it). | fixed | [scripts/mutation_guard.sh](../../scripts/mutation_guard.sh) | AT:R66 |

So: retry GETs only (idempotent by verb), or give `evaluate` an idempotency key before it is ever retried; never a verb-blind interceptor. Then (a) state the definition and an admissible range in the PM contract, anchored to the evidence actually supplied; (b) add a deterministic coherence check beside the existing geometry annotations in `room_runner` — a stop whose distance from entry is implausible for the stated horizon is a contradiction the code should catch, exactly as `_verify_and_annotate_geometry` already catches R:R contradictions; (c) decide whether the board should render a thesis horizon at all when the stop will resolve the position far sooner. **Acceptance:** re-run the CR164 pinned regression batch and require that no approval pairs a horizon > 365 days with a stop closer than the ticker's own realized volatility over that horizon, with the residual hand-read; and that the rendered board copy no longer states an investment horizon as if it were the trade's expected duration. Tier A under CR142 if the fix touches prompt bytes — owes the audit handshake.  **FIXED 2026-08-11 (AT:R68, Batch 8).** Two halves, because a prompt line is not a control (P2). **The definition:** `_PM_VERDICT_FORMAT` now states `horizon_days` is *"how long THIS trade needs to work out, not the user's investment horizon"* and anchors the admissible range to the evidence actually supplied — 3 months of price history, TTM fundamentals, a 52-week range — noting that a multi-year number is supported by nothing on the fact sheet. **The control:** `_horizon_coherence_note` fires deterministically beside the existing geometry annotations when a stated horizon exceeds `_MAX_EVIDENCED_HORIZON_DAYS = 365`. | DEF259 | 2026-08-11 | games | **A game position could be opened and never closed — the game was one-way, and the only exit was the run ending.** Found by Saiful playing the shipped build: *"how do I close an open trade I have? I want to sell (or buy, if I short) tickers during the day"*. The answer was that he couldn't. The backend has supported SELL since slice 2 (`GameTradeRequest.side: Side = Side.BUY` accepts `sell`; `_execute_fill` has a full sell branch), and the ticket's own notifier carried a `pickSide` method — **called from nowhere**: `grep -rn 'pickSide' mobile/lib mobile/test` returned exactly its own definition at `games_providers.dart:217`. `side` was hard-coded to `'buy'`, and there was no sell affordance on any of the eight games screens (0 hits for `setSide`/`SELL`/`sell` across `mobile/lib/screens/games/*.dart`). In a contest scored on P&L that is not a missing convenience, it is a missing half of the game. **The subtle half of the fix: a buy and a sell divide different things.** A buy divides CASH — 25% is a quarter of what is available to deploy. A sell divides the POSITION — 25% is a quarter of the shares held, 100% closes it. Sizing a sell against cash would be nonsense in the ordinary case and *impossible* in the important one: a player whose cash is fully committed to queued orders has exactly 0 to size against, and closing a position is the one action they most need — the exact state Saiful was in on build 78 with 10,003.29 committed and 0.00 available. Shares rather than a dollar round-trip is deliberate: re-deriving the count from a price lands a few thousandths off, which at 100% is the difference between closing a position and leaving a dust holding behind. The null-vs-zero split is applied on the new axis too — a null `heldQuantity` means the holdings have not arrived (wait), zero means there is nothing to sell (an answer, ending in a drawable state); that is the ninth-instance bug class this feature keeps producing one level down. SELL sits on each position ROW rather than as one button, because the thing being sold is a specific position. Copy is separated the same way the arithmetic is: `gamesTicketStepSizeSell` ("HOW MUCH OF THE POSITION") and `gamesTicketSizeCloseAll` ("Close it") rather than reusing the buy step's label and "All in", which means the opposite thing. **Shorting stays refused** — `_execute_fill` rejects a sell beyond the held quantity (`cannot sell {quantity} {ticker}: not enough held`), so a sell only ever closes or reduces a long; that is the shared fill path's rule, not a games-specific one, and it is now stated on the ticket instead of being discovered as a rejected order. **Verification:** `mobile/test/screens/games/games_sell_path_test.dart`, 9 tests, incl. the zero-available-cash case (mutation-checked: removing the `!_isSell` guard turns it red), an assertion that the quote carries `quantity` and not a notional, and a notifier test proving a side switch clears the size because the percentage changes meaning. | DEF269 | 2026-08-11 | bug:tester-report | sim | **Game fills leaked into every TRAINING read of `sim_trades` — and `evaluate_outcomes` sold them out of the training portfolio.** Reported by a tester on the shipped build: *"game trades are appearing in portfolio open trades."* `sim_trades` was a per-USER table long before it was a per-portfolio one. Two quieter halves: `_risk_limit_context` reads `list_trades`, so game fills consumed the training account's over-trading brake, post-loss cooldown and open-risk cap — the safety floor refusing a training trade on activity that never happened in the account it protects; and `holding_lots` blended game fills into a training holding's FIFO cost basis, producing a wrong average cost on a screen the user reads as fact. `day_trader_outcomes._load_all_trades` had the same shape (a lesson about the user's own practice account, counting their contest fills). **Fix:** one `training_trade_scope(user_id)` clause — `SimTradeRow.portfolio_id.in_(select(SimPortfolioRow.id).where(user_id, kind == "training"))` — applied at all six sites. Scoping by `portfolio_id` rather than by a new `kind` column on the trade is deliberate: the portfolio row already knows its lane, so there is nothing to keep in sync and no way to write a trade whose own label disagrees with the portfolio it belongs to. Mutation-checked: reverting `training_trade_scope` to `user_id ==` turns 6 of the 8 red. | DEF270 | 2026-08-12 | prompt | sim | **The anonymous→claimed merge dropped the whole career: a player's career-point total silently became ZERO at the moment they signed up.** `merge_service.execute` re-keys 24 tables and missed three, all of which the game depends on. **`career_events` is the severe one.** `career_ledger.career_points_total` is `SUM(delta)` over that table for a `user_id`, so leaving the rows on the dead orphan account does not merely lose a history — the adopted account's career score, and every title and rung derived from it, reads as 0. A player who played a week anonymously and then claimed their account would watch their score vanish at the exact moment the product asks them to commit, and the runs themselves DID move (`game_entries`, `game_portfolios`, `game_trades`, `portfolio_nav_daily` are all handled), so every surface anyone looks at would have appeared to work. **`game_duels` is the subtle one — THREE user columns, not two.** `_rekey_all` only knows a `user_id` column, so it cannot reach a table that names a user on each side; and beyond `user_a_id`/`user_b_id`, `winner_user_id` is a separate pointer. Moving the sides while leaving the winner behind is WORSE than losing the row: the adopted account ends up in a settled duel it did not win, i.e. a fabricated loss on its record. (That half-fix was written, then caught by its own mutation check before it shipped.) Leaving duels behind entirely also breaks `games_duels.opponent_of()`, which decides which side is "you" by comparing `user_a_id == user_id` — against a stale id it falls through and returns side A, so a claimed account's duel card would show the player **their own book as the opponent**. **`game_short_positions` is the quiet one:** every read is by `portfolio_id` and the portfolio does move, so the position keeps working and the row simply carries a dead owner until some future user-scoped query needs it — exactly why it would not have been noticed. **A trap in the obvious fix, recorded because it would have looked like success:** reusing the existing `_rekey_skipping_conflicts(conflict_col=period_key)` for `career_events` is silently wrong — `period_key` is NULL on every non-stipend row and `NULL NOT IN (...)` evaluates to NULL (falsy), so every `run_close` and every `duel_result` row would have been left behind while the merge reported a non-zero count. Hence a dedicated `_rekey_career_events` that moves everything and drops only a `finish_stipend` row whose `period_key` the adopter has already claimed (`uq_career_event_stipend_period` is the one genuine conflict; adopter wins, matching every other conflict on this path). **Verification:** `backend/tests/unit/test_games_merge_career_and_duels.py`, 9 tests, incl. the orphan-on-side-B case, the winner-pointer case (mutation-checked: removing that one `update` turns 2 red), the stipend conflict AND its mutation guard that a DIFFERENT period still moves, and a closing test written as an INVARIANT — *nothing the player earned stays on the dead account* — rather than as a list of tables, because two of the three tables here were added the same day the gap was found and a table-by-table test goes stale the next time the game grows one. The rows are still returned, renamed `rows_for_hand_reading`. (3) **Two alternative sources were measured before giving up, not assumed away:** the CR106 stance envelope carries a size in **1 of 54** risk turns (2%), and the transcript entry has no structured size field at all (`agent_id`/`content`/`conviction`/`headline`/`model`/`role`/`stance`/`timestamp`/`token_count`). So restoring M4 as a real metric needs the agents to *declare* size in the envelope — a prompt change, not a parser change — and that is recorded rather than done, since it adds prompt bytes and DEF236 binds. **What is NOT claimed:** no guard yet stops the next import drift from crashing this script; the honest fix is a smoke test that runs the sweep against the committed epoch in CI, and it is not built here. | DEF273 | 2026-08-12 | prompt | games | **The game's order queue accepted orders the run could never pay for, and only said so hours later by cancelling them.** `games_service.submit_trade`'s out-of-hours branch wrote a `GameQueuedOrderRow` with **no affordability check of any kind** — it stored whatever it was handed. A player could commit several times their book overnight; the FIFO drain then filled what fit and cancelled the rest with `rejected at fill time`, at the next open, on a screen nobody was looking at. Saiful had already hit the shape of this on build 78 (*"I have 10,003.29 committed to 8 queued orders, 0.00 available"*), and the fixes it produced — `cash_available` on the ticket, and the drain's explicit FIFO `ORDER BY` — each addressed a different half: the ticket stopped *offering* the whole stake twice, and the drain stopped letting undefined row order decide which orders survived. **Neither told the player at the moment they placed the order**, which is the only moment they could act on it. **Fix:** `_refuse_overcommitted_queue` runs before the row is written, prices the order at read time, and refuses when `estimate > current_cash − already_committed`, naming BOTH numbers plus what is already committed. The estimate includes the fee, because quoting the bare notional understates what the order needs — that is how a player retries at a size that is still one fee too big. **Two exemptions, each a worse defect if got wrong.** A **SELL** is never refused: it returns cash and is precisely the order a player most needs from an empty balance — the one-way book DEF259 had to fix. A **COVER** is never refused either (a buy on a name with a standing short), because Amendment G ruling 5 makes it structural: the cash to buy back was posted at open, and a cover blocked for want of cash traps a player in the one position whose loss is unbounded. The cover case is decided from the same standing-short fact the fill path uses, so the two cannot disagree about what the order is. **The market-hours fence is not breached:** that fence exists so an order never FILLS at a stale price, and this is an estimate used to REFUSE, never to fill — nothing is stored, and the fill still happens at the next open's price. Because an estimate can be wrong by a weekend's drift, the drain keeps its own check; this makes the common case honest, it does not replace the authority at fill time. **With no usable price (`price <= 0`) the check stands down and logs** rather than guessing — a refusal built on a fabricated number is the CR040 class, and it is the same "no usable price" condition `quote_trade` already refuses on. **Verification:** `backend/tests/unit/test_def273_queue_overcommitment.py`, 8 tests incl. the two-orders-each-affordable-alone sequence that is Saiful's actual case, an assertion that the refusal names both numbers *with the fee included*, and the sell/cover exemptions. Mutation-checked: removing the sell/cover exemption turns the sell test red. Full suite 3,610 passed, 1 skipped. **A test-harness trap worth recording:** the first version of this file constructed `SimEngine(provider=...)` and asserted exact prices — but `conftest` nulls `sim_engine._engine` per test and `submit_trade` resolves through `get_sim_engine()`, so the code under test ran on a mock-walk price while the test measured nothing. Related: CR109 slice 2 (the queue), DEF259, CR109 Amendment G ruling 5. | fixed | backend/app/services/games_service.py · backend/tests/unit/test_def273_queue_overcommitment.py | AT:R66 |

| DEF304 | 2026-08-14 | logic | backend | **The DEF136 loop-responsiveness guard goes red on correct code when the machine is busy, so the one test that can prove the Room's convene path is not freezing every other user's stream is also a test that cries wolf.** Found while producing the CR179 audit evidence: the same suite, at the same SHA (`86d9af99`), in the same clean worktree, ran twice and gave `4106 passed, 3 skipped` exit 0 and then `1 failed, 4105 passed, 3 skipped` exit 1. **Isolated and measured before filing** (DEF279/P19 — a metric's first number is a hypothesis about the metric): `test_the_loop_never_stalls_while_the_builders_block` run 5× on unchanged code at load average 3.0 → **1 failure**, `AssertionError: the event loop STALLED for 0.273s in a single gap (threshold 0.150s)`. **The arithmetic error is one term.** The guard drives a convene with both portfolio builders replaced by probes that `time.sleep(_BLOCK_S)`, and watches the longest gap between heartbeat ticks. Only the second term is a constant — but the threshold was the bare constant `_BLOCK_S / 2 = 0.150s`, measured on an idle Mac and hardcoded. Once `jitter` alone approaches 0.15s the guard fails without any regression, and at `jitter` 0.273s it is not even close. Under load both terms rise together and the ~10× separation survives; on an idle box the baseline is ~0.01s and the threshold is what it always was. A second assertion guards the baseline itself — a baseline at or above `_BLOCK_S / 2` makes the first assertion unfalsifiable, so the test now says *"this machine is too loaded for the measurement to mean anything, and this is not a DEF136 regression"* rather than passing vacuously, which is the CR040 degrade-loudly distinction applied to a test. **Verified, not asserted:** fixed guard 6/6 green; un-wrapping `room_runner.py:3874`'s `await asyncio.to_thread(_build_sim_holdings_block, ...)` fails **both** halves 3/3.
